lesson.title: Faking Out the Flag Pattern: How Bit Stuffing Works
lesson.summary: Bit stuffing inserts extra 0 bits into a data stream whenever five consecutive 1 bits appear, so protocols like HDLC and PPP can safely use a reserved flag pattern for framing without ever confusing it with ordinary payload data.
lesson.body:
Framing schemes that use a special bit pattern to mark the start and end of a frame run into an obvious problem: what happens when the data being transmitted happens to contain that exact same pattern. A receiver has no way to tell a coincidental match in the payload from a genuine frame boundary unless the protocol does something to prevent the ambiguity in the first place. Bit stuffing is the classic bit level solution, used by protocols such as HDLC and PPP when operating over a synchronous, bit oriented link.

HDLC and PPP use the 8 bit flag pattern 01111110 to mark both the start and end of every frame, a pattern whose defining feature is six consecutive 1 bits. The bit stuffing rule is simple: whenever the transmitter is about to send five consecutive 1 bits in the actual data, it inserts, or stuffs, an extra 0 bit immediately afterward, regardless of what the next real data bit would have been. Because a real flag can only ever appear as six 1s bounded by 0s, and stuffed data can now never contain more than five consecutive 1s in a row, the receiver can always tell a genuine flag apart from ordinary payload. It just has to count.

Walk through a concrete example. Suppose the data to transmit is the 6 bit sequence 111110. As the transmitter sends the first five bits, it counts five consecutive 1s in a row, so immediately after that fifth 1 it stuffs in an extra 0, and only then continues with the original sixth bit, which happens to be a 0. The transmitted, stuffed sequence becomes 1111100, seven bits instead of six. On the receiving end, the receiver also counts consecutive 1 bits as they arrive. The moment it sees five 1s followed by a 0, it knows that 0 was artificially inserted and discards it, recovering the original 111110 exactly. Because this rule is applied consistently to every run of five 1s anywhere in the data, including runs that were never going to form an actual flag pattern, the receiver never has to guess, it simply removes every stuffed 0 it finds after five consecutive 1s and keeps the rest.

This technique costs a small amount of overhead, since occasional extra bits get added to the transmitted stream, but that overhead is tiny for typical data and it completely eliminates the ambiguity that framing depends on avoiding. The worst case overhead is bounded and predictable: since a stuff bit is inserted for every five consecutive 1 bits, data that happens to be a long run of nothing but 1s expands by one extra bit for every five original bits, a 20 percent increase in size, while ordinary, more varied data expands by far less because long runs of five consecutive 1s are comparatively rare.

Bit stuffing operates purely at the level of individual bits and does not care about byte boundaries at all, which distinguishes it from the closely related technique covered next, byte stuffing, that solves the exact same problem for protocols organized around whole bytes rather than a raw bit stream.
